new.title: Pick a Belgian beer at De Pintelier
new.desc: De Pintelier started out as the first Belgian café in Groningen and has been a fixture for more than 25 years. It pours around 30 beers on tap, keeps about 80 bottles and cans as a fixed range, and rotates through more than 250 guest beers over a year, trappists included.
new.tip: The staff are happy to steer you if you name a flavour rather than a brand. It sits in a narrow lane just off the Vismarkt, so it is easy to walk past.
new.q: De Pintelier Kleine Kromme Elleboog Groningen

new.title: Walk along the houseboats of the Noorderhaven
new.desc: Where the Aa runs into the Reitdiep lies the Noorderhaven, known as the last free harbour in the Netherlands: ships may moor wherever there is space. Old barges and lived-in houseboats lie hull to hull below the quay houses, between the Visserbrug, the Kijk in 't Jatbrug and the Plantsoenbrug.
new.tip: Walk the north side for the best view back to the gables of the south quay. The city has decided the harbour should in time be kept for well-maintained historic ships, so the mix of boats is slowly changing.

new.title: Sit under the lime trees at Café de Minnaar
new.desc: In one of the prettiest lanes of the Hortusbuurt, Café de Minnaar van de Rozenstraat has been the neighbourhood's living room since 1996. City historian Beno Hofman traced a café on this spot back to about 1886, when Renske Bart was registered here as a 'tapster'.
new.tip: The terrace sits under three big lime trees and catches the afternoon sun. The café opens daily from mid afternoon and runs pub quizzes, card evenings and live music, so check the agenda.
new.q: Café de Minnaar Kleine Rozenstraat Groningen

new.title: Order the namesake cocktail at Bramble
new.desc: A tired brown café opposite the Noorderplantsoen was reborn in 2018 as Bramble, a small cocktail and wine bar run by a couple and their two daughters. It is named after the cocktail of gin, lemon and blackberry liqueur that Dick Bradsell invented in London in 1984.
new.tip: It is closed on Monday and Tuesday and opens mid afternoon on the other days. In summer the tables move onto former parking spaces, with a view of the park.

new.title: Throw a round of boules at BOEL
new.desc: On the edge of the Noorderplantsoen, BOEL is Groningen's jeu de boules bar: indoor lanes where you play pétanque with a drink in your hand and food on the side. No ball skills are needed, and it also runs its own pub quiz.
new.tip: Reserve a lane in advance, especially on Friday and Saturday evenings. It opens in the late afternoon, so combine it with a walk through the park first.

new.title: Catch a rising act at Simplon
new.desc: Simplon is Groningen's stage for new talent, in an early twentieth century brick factory on the Boterdiep that once canned meat and later made raincoats under the Simplon label. Squatting hippies and artists began holding concerts here in the 1970s, and punk ruled in the 1980s. The main hall has a sunken floor called 'de kuil', which keeps shows close and intimate.
new.tip: The programme now leans to hip-hop, dance and pop newcomers. Tickets for the small-stage nights are cheap, so take a chance on a name you do not know.

new.title: Step through the Ming garden at the Hortus in Haren
new.desc: The botanical garden of Groningen dates from the seventeenth century and moved from the city to Haren in 1967. It now covers more than 14 hectares, with a Chinese Ming garden that is unique in Europe, a rock garden, a herb garden and the wild Laarman garden, an ecological monument.
new.tip: Haren is a short train or bus ride from Groningen, or an easy flat ride by bike. Opening hours are shorter in winter, so check the day before you go.

new.title: See the city from a canal boat
new.desc: The family firm Kool has been running canal tours since 1969 from the quay opposite the main station. The city tour takes an hour through the Groningen canals with an audio guide in several languages. The boats are hybrid and glide along almost silently.
new.tip: In the dark months there is a candlelight cruise with glühwein and oliebollen past the lit bridges and towers. A longer tour heads out along the Reitdiep.

new.title: Watch an arthouse film in the old hospital
new.desc: The former Roman Catholic hospital in Helpman, opened in 1925, was squatted on 3 September 1979 and legalised in 1985. About 250 people now live in the Oude RKZ, which also holds studios, a day café, a pub and RKZbios, a small cinema showing arthouse films and documentaries.
new.tip: The box office opens half an hour before the film and tickets cost less than at the big cinemas. Enter from the Emmastraat side.

new.title: Eat pancakes on board the Johanna
new.desc: The pancake ship Johanna was built in 1939 as a motor cargo vessel. On the day of her trial run the Dutch mobilisation was announced, so she was rented to the Red Cross as a medical ship, and she later came through the war unscathed by moving from hiding place to hiding place. Now a 50 metre three-master, she seats 240 guests.
new.tip: You only need to reserve for groups of seven or more; smaller parties can just walk in. The ship closes for a week of maintenance now and then, so check before a special trip.

new.title: Share a Lebanese mezze table at Fatoush
new.desc: On the Damsterdiep, just east of the centre, Fatoush has been cooking Lebanese recipes handed down through the generations since 2016. The heart of the menu is the mezza, a generous table of warm and cold small dishes to share, with plenty for vegetarians.
new.tip: Come with at least three or four people so you can order a wide spread. Leave room for the Lebanese sweets at the end.

new.title: Count the clocks on the Drunkard's Tower
new.desc: The neo-Gothic Sint-Jozefkathedraal was built between 1885 and 1887 to a design by Pierre Cuypers and has been the cathedral of the diocese since 1981. Its 78 metre tower is six-sided, so from any direction you see at least two clock faces at once. Stadjers call it the Dronkemanstoren, because it makes you think you are seeing double.
new.tip: The church was dedicated to Joseph, patron of workers, for the labourers of the nearby Oosterpoort. Step inside for the painted choir and the high altar by Mengelberg.

new.title: Climb the Kardingebult for a view over the city
new.desc: Between Beijum and Lewenborg lies Kardinge, a nature and recreation area managed by Natuurmonumenten with woods, meadows, lakes and marsh. In the middle rises the Kardingebult, an artificial hill about 30 metres above sea level, with paths to a lookout at the top. The Bevrijdingsbos nearby honours the Canadians who liberated Groningen in 1945 and has a pond with an island shaped like a maple leaf.
new.tip: On a warm day bring swimming gear for the Zilvermeer. The sports centre next door has the city's ice rink and a climbing tower if the weather turns.

new.title: Taste Maallust beer in the prison village of Veenhuizen
new.desc: Brewery Maallust works in the old grain mill of Veenhuizen, the colony where paupers and later prisoners were put to work from the 1820s. Farm produce from the colony was once processed here, and old machinery and notes scribbled on the beams still recall those days of order and labour. The taproom pours the beers fresh, a few steps from the kettles.
new.tip: The taproom is closed on Monday and Tuesday. Book a tour with tasting if you want to see the brewhouse, and pair your visit with the prison museum nearby.

new.title: Go behind bars at the Gevangenismuseum in Veenhuizen
new.desc: The National Prison Museum fills the Tweede Gesticht of 1823, built by the Society of Benevolence to house and reform the poor. Inside are leg irons, a straitjacket, cell doors from different periods and the ledgers in which the debts and earnings of colony orphans were written down. Veenhuizen is part of the Colonies of Benevolence, a UNESCO World Heritage site.
new.tip: Reserve a seat on the old prisoner transport bus, which tours the village. Allow at least half a day for the museum and the village together.

new.title: Warm up by the stove at 't Zielhoes
new.desc: Noordpolderzijl is the smallest sea harbour in the Netherlands, reachable by boat only at high tide through a shallow channel that falls completely dry at ebb. At the foot of the sea dike, the former sluice keeper's house is the nostalgic brown café 't Zielhoes, with a pot stove inside and a terrace outside. The old sluice dates from 1811.
new.tip: Order a shrimp sandwich, or on a raw day a glass of 'kwast' by the stove. Climb the dike first for the view over the salt marsh and the Wadden Sea.

new.title: Lose yourself in the maze of the Menkemaborg
new.desc: The Menkemaborg in Uithuizen is one of the few surviving Groningen borgen, the manor houses of the landed gentry. The house goes back to around 1400, was extended into a U-shape in 1614 and remodelled around 1700, and is furnished as in the eighteenth century. The formal garden holds one of the few historic mazes in the country.
new.tip: The former cattle barn, the Schathoes, is now a restaurant, good for lunch after the gardens. Check the opening days before you travel, as they vary with the season.

new.title: Dig into a thousand years of mound life in Ezinge
new.desc: Ezinge sits on a wierde, a dwelling mound raised against the sea. Between 1923 and 1934 the archaeologist Albert van Giffen cut it open and found the remains of 85 farmhouses and 60 outbuildings, dating from about 600 BC to the fifth century AD. Museum Wierdenland tells that story and shows finds from the mound landscape of the northern coast.
new.tip: After the museum, walk up to the thirteenth century church with its free-standing tower on the edge of the excavated mound. The lanes of Middag-Humsterland around the village make a fine bike loop.

new.title: Trace peat, ships and potato starch in Veendam
new.desc: The Veenkoloniaal Museum, founded in 1939, explains how the peat colonies were dug out and what came after: potato starch and strawboard factories, and a surprising seafaring trade that has a Riga room of its own. It is housed in a former secondary school of 1911. The museum also keeps the Familietrouw, a peat barge built in Veendam in 1894.
new.tip: Ask about the guided town walks. The heritage railway to Stadskanaal starts in the same town, so the two combine well.

new.title: Ride a steam train through the peat colonies
new.desc: Museumspoorlijn STAR calls itself the longest heritage railway in the Netherlands, running between Veendam, Stadskanaal and Musselkanaal on the border of Groningen and Drenthe. The foundation has kept the line alive since 1992 and hauls trains with heavy German steam locomotives built in 1943. The workshop and depot are at Stadskanaal station.
new.tip: Trains only run on selected days, so check the timetable first. Ordinary tickets need no booking, but special days and arrangements do.

new.title: Walk the bare dunes of the Aekingerzand
new.desc: In the Drents-Friese Wold national park, right on the border of Drenthe and Friesland, lies a wide stretch of drifting sand known as the Kale Duinen, the bare dunes. To keep the sand moving, around 200 hectares of forest were felled at the end of the twentieth century. A shepherd's flock grazes the heath, and it is the last inland breeding site of the northern wheatear in the country.
new.tip: Come early or late in the day, when the sand ridges throw long shadows. Dogs are not allowed from 1 March to 1 September because of the breeding birds.
